title: This is why you don't have a Demon Back (Advanced Tips)
summary: NH reviews a 16-year-old creator's (Randumb Fitness) back-training video and adds advanced tips: pick 1-2 exercises per area and progress them in set rep ranges, use straps, don't obsess over the deadlift, follow strict pull-up rules, keep technique standardized when overloading, and spread back work across the week instead of a back day.
claims: The back is made of several muscle groups, but that doesn't require many variations per area; pick 1-2 exercises and get strong on them in relevant rep ranges
Constantly rotating back exercises (e.g. every two months) means relearning the pattern and never grinding through plateaus
Pull-ups: sets of 3-5 (5x5 or 3x3 also work); other pull-up variations 6-10
Barbell rows 3-5 reps to push intensity, or 6-10 if unsure of your technique; 6-10 also for hip hinges
Hip hinges like good mornings and RDLs also thicken the erectors and rhomboids; only doing pull-ups leaves you flat as paper from the side
Pulldowns and dumbbell/chest-supported/cable rows work best at 8-12 to push to failure; rear-delt isolation and shrugs 10-15
Most back exercises train several muscles at once, so don't panic about leaving gains on the table
No need for dedicated lower-back slots unless injured; heavy rows and hinges already develop it
Pulling doesn't develop the forearms fully, and letting grip limit the back is criminal; strap up as soon as grip fails on a set
Pulldowns and diagonal pulls where you lock the bar don't need straps; use them only when needed and train forearms directly
The claim that grip work steals CNS recruitment from the back is bro science
Don't bother with mixed or hook grip for deadlifts; hook grip exists because weightlifters can't use straps, so just use straps
The deadlift recruits the most muscle but that makes it fatiguing, not better for back growth; people who obsessed over it for years were disappointed with their backs
If you deadlift three times a week, cut it to once and spend the energy on pull-ups or rows
After a year, the pull-up trainee will have the more aesthetic back; the deadlifter may be thicker, so do both hinges and pull-ups
Pull-up rule 1: the negative must always be slower than the positive; most of the gains happen while resisting gravity on the way down
Pull-up rule 2: start every rep from the top so the first thing you do is the negative
Pull-up rule 3: stay under the bar and keep it in line with your body; leaning back and curving away turns it into an arm movement
Dead-hang pull-ups aren't necessary; the passive stretch at the bottom isn't worth it, while the active stretch is what matters
Expect strict pull-ups to cost reps and load on weighted pull-ups, but the hypertrophy is better
Barbell rows drift into a hip hinge as you add plates; a strict one-plate rower can be twice your size
On lat pulldowns don't lean way back or bring the arms forward; pull in line with the cable
Progressive overload is useless unless reps, technique and tempo are standardized, because changing form breaks the link between load and muscle stress
The back is the most undertrained muscle group with the biggest potential; the best natural backs belong to lifters in their 30s-40s
Being big, the back needs the most volume and training over time
Don't have a back day: split six back exercises as two on Monday, two on Wednesday and two on Saturday
Synergistic planning: train traps with posterior chain, and lats with biceps after a heavy weighted chin-up
Rear delts do badly on shoulder day; train them on lower-body days and your progress will skyrocket
Pullovers (dumbbell, machine, or cable on a bench with a low pulley, even on a decline) are his favourite lift and pair best with push days
A 16-year-old giving basic, sound advice beats most adult YouTube fitness creators, many of whom are on drugs
